name: Hair-growth inhibitor lotion
lead: Hair-growth inhibitor lotions are topical products used to slow how quickly unwanted facial or body hair comes back after shaving, waxing or plucking. People use them to keep skin smoother for longer between hair-removal sessions, to cut down on shadow and stubble, and to reduce the visible upkeep of a clean-shaven or hair-free look. The term covers a prescription cream and a range of over-the-counter lotions sold as hair retardants or inhibitors.

The best-documented active ingredient is eflornithine, sold as a prescription facial cream (brand name Vaniqa) for women with excess facial hair. It blocks an enzyme in the hair follicle called ornithine decarboxylase, which slows the growth of the hair rather than removing it [1]. Wikipedia reports that in clinical studies 81% of women showed improvement after twelve months, that results began to appear around eight weeks, and that hair returned to baseline within about eight weeks of stopping [1]. Eflornithine has also been used as a reference hair-growth inhibitor in laboratory work on human hair follicles [2].

Over-the-counter retardant lotions are a looser category. Their ingredients differ by brand, and Wikipedia's hair-removal article lists them among non-prescription methods sold with limited published clinical data [3].

chain: Lotion is applied to skin after shaving or waxing
Follicle activity is slowed (eflornithine blocks ornithine decarboxylase)
Hair regrows more slowly, so skin stays smooth longer
angle.text: Users apply the product to areas such as the face, lip or body after hair removal so the hair reappears more slowly and the smooth look lasts longer between sessions. The prescription cream is described as reducing the psychological burden of facial hair for women who have it [1]. The effect lasts only while the product is used.

infobox: Hair returns to baseline within about 8 weeks of stopping [1]
Eflornithine cream is prescription-only in the US [1]

paras: Eflornithine acts as a suicide inhibitor of ornithine decarboxylase, an enzyme needed for cell growth in the hair follicle; it binds the enzyme irreversibly [1]. It is described as the only prescription topical treatment that slows facial hair growth [1]. Wikipedia reports that it significantly reduced the psychological burden of facial hirsutism in studies [1]. Normal hair removal such as shaving or depilation can continue alongside treatment [3].
Acne is the most commonly reported side effect, at 7 to 14%. Ingrown-hair skin reactions, stinging, burning or tingling, dryness, itching, redness and rash have also been reported [1].

Non-prescription products sold as hair retardants, inhibitors or growth reducers are typically used after shaving or waxing. Their active ingredients vary by brand. Wikipedia's hair-removal article groups these preparations among methods sold without published clinical proof of the claimed effect [3].

Merrell Dow Research Institute developed eflornithine in the late 1970s as a cancer treatment. It did not work against malignancies, but researchers observed that it strongly reduced hair growth, and it was also found to treat African sleeping sickness. It was registered for that use in 1990 [1]. The topical cream later received marketing approval from the US FDA and the European Commission for facial hair in women [1].

Antiandrogen medicines such as spironolactone and finasteride are used by prescribers for unwanted hair in women. They can slow facial hair and prevent new hair, but have little effect on existing facial hair [3]. They are a different category from topical lotions.

No studies found for over-the-counter hair-growth inhibitor lotions. For prescription eflornithine, clinical studies reported improvement in 81% of women after twelve months, with hair regrowth to baseline after stopping [1]. A laboratory study of human hair follicles in culture used eflornithine as a clinically used topical hair-growth inhibitor and found that it induced premature entry into the regression phase (catagen) [2].

timeline.event: Merrell Dow Research Institute develops eflornithine as a cancer drug and observes reduced hair growth [1].
Eflornithine is registered for gambiense sleeping sickness [1].

card.summary: Lotions that slow hair regrowth: one Rx ingredient (eflornithine) has trial data, OTC versions have little.
card.note: Effect reverses after stopping; OTC formulations vary and are unstudied here.

quick.overview:
These lotions aim to slow how fast unwanted hair comes back. The prescription version, eflornithine cream, is used for facial hair in women and has clinical data behind it.

Over-the-counter retardant lotions are a loose category with varied ingredients, and no trials of them were found.
quick.mechanism: Eflornithine blocks an enzyme (ornithine decarboxylase) in the follicle, which slows hair growth rather than removing hair.
quick.risks: Acne, stinging, itching and rash are reported with eflornithine. Hair regrows to baseline within about eight weeks of stopping.
